strengths: Compelling training-free paradigm: The paper shows that off-the-shelf MLLMs can achieve competitive or superior retrieval performance compared to heavily supervised models trained on millions of multimodal pairs (e.g., matching or exceeding UniME and outperforming GME and MMRet).

Insightful analysis of representation bottlenecks: The probing analysis of 'lexicalization pressure' in Section 3.2 convincingly shows that the final MLP layer sharply shifts representations toward token prediction rather than semantic abstractions, providing a solid empirical justification for taking features before the final MLP ($h_L^{Attn}$).

Identification and mitigation of the LLM framing effect: Documenting the sensitivity of point-wise reranking to logically equivalent prompt wordings (Yes/No vs. Right/Wrong vs. True/False) and resolving this via neutral multiple-choice framing (MCQ) is an effective and well-demonstrated contribution.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The method is validated across 46 datasets spanning MMEB and MMEB-V2 video subsets, across multiple model families (Qwen-VL, InternVL, LLaVA) and parameter scales (2B to 32B), accompanied by clear component ablations.
weaknesses: Unbalanced comparison against single-stage bi-encoders: In Table 1, FreeRet (a two-stage system combining embedding retrieval and top-k pointwise reranking) is compared against single-stage dense retrievers (e.g., GME, mmE5, UniME). As shown in Table 3 and Figure 5, embedding-only FreeRet achieves ~53.7% on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, while reranking brings it to 70.7%. Comparing the full two-stage pipeline directly against single-stage encoders without explicitly clarifying the architectural disparity in Table 1 can be misleading.

Inference latency and computational cost: Evaluating up to 50 candidates per query using a full 7B or 32B MLLM for reranking entails substantial FLOPs and latency. Although Section A.5 qualitatively mentions this bottleneck, quantitative profiling (e.g., query latency, wall-clock time, and GPU memory usage relative to standard rerankers) is absent.

Triviality of the theoretical analysis: Appendix A.2 frames standard cross-entropy gradient properties with respect to a linear classifier as a formal Lemma and Corollary, which adds little mathematical insight beyond the well-known fact that CE loss updates align features with target vocabulary weights.

Sensitivity to prompt formatting: The controlled generation relies on handcrafted instructions (semantic grounding, noise suppression, and task priors). A broader evaluation of robustness against prompt paraphrasing across diverse multimodal tasks would strengthen the generalizability claims.

strengths: Compelling and insightful analysis of 'lexicalization pressure': The authors identify that the final MLP layer right before the language modeling head sharply shifts intermediate representations toward token prediction logits at the expense of semantic richness. Demonstrating that bypassing the final MLP layer ($h_L^{Attn}$) consistently improves retrieval performance across multiple architectures and model scales is a simple yet impactful finding.

Systematic and effective prompt-level improvements: The proposed controlled generation prompting (introducing task alignment, semantic grounding, and noise suppression) substantially refines embedding quality without requiring parameter updates.

Identification and mitigation of the LLM framing effect in reranking: Revealing the sensitivity of MLLM-based binary rerankers to surface verbalizers (e.g., Yes/No vs. True/False) and showing that casting reranking as a multiple-choice question (MCQ) neutralizes lexical bias is novel and practically useful.

Extensive and rigorous evaluation: The method is validated across 36 datasets on MMEB and video tasks on MMEB-V2 across diverse model families (Qwen, InternVL, LLaVA) and scales (2B to 32B), demonstrating strong improvements over existing training-free baselines and competitive performance against heavily fine-tuned retrievers.
weaknesses: Confounding between two-stage pipeline and pure embedding baselines: FreeRet is an end-to-end two-stage retriever (embedding search + pointwise MLLM reranking). Many baselines in Table 1 (such as VLM2Vec, GME, MMRet, and E5-V) are single-stage embedding/dual-encoder models. As shown in Table 3 and Figure 5, reranking alone accounts for a massive boost (e.g., from ~53.7% to 70.7% on Qwen2.5-VL-7B). Table 1 would be clearer and fairer if it explicitly separated single-stage first-pass retrieval performance from the two-stage (retrieve + rerank) performance of both FreeRet and comparable pipelines.

Lack of inference efficiency and latency profiling: Performing point-wise MLLM reranking over top-$k$ candidates (e.g., $k=20$ or $50$) using large models (7B, 32B) introduces considerable computational latency compared to dense retrieval. While the authors discuss massive-candidate scalability qualitatively in Appendix A.5, quantitative benchmarks of latency, FLOPs, or throughput during inference should be provided.

Minor typographical errors in the text: In Section 3.3, several typos appear in the prompt design constraints (e.g., 'stear' instead of 'steer', 'reqired' instead of 'required', and 'concent' instead of 'content').

strengths: Practical and accessible training-free formulation: The paper tackles the high computational and data costs of training multimodal retrievers by proposing a plug-and-play, parameter-free pipeline using off-the-shelf MLLMs.

Insightful empirical probing on lexicalization pressure: The analysis in Section 3.2 and Figure 2 systematically investigates representational distortion across transformer layers, demonstrating that the final MLP disproportionately projects representations into discrete lexical space at the expense of semantic continuity.

Identification of the framing effect in zero-shot reranking: The observation that semantically equivalent binary labels (e.g., Right/Wrong vs. Yes/No vs. MCQ) introduce substantial variance due to pretraining frequency biases is insightful, and framing reranking as an MCQ provides a simple and effective mitigation.

Extensive benchmark coverage across architectures: Experiments cover 46 datasets spanning MMEB and MMEB-V2 video benchmarks, as well as multiple distinct MLLM backbones (Qwen2-VL, Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3, and LLaVA-OV) and downstream long-video tasks (LVBench).
weaknesses: Confounded and asymmetric comparison against baseline models: In Table 1, FreeRet is presented as outperforming or matching heavily trained supervised retrievers. However, FreeRet operates as a two-stage pipeline (embedding retrieval followed by pointwise MLLM reranking over top-50 candidates), whereas almost all baselines (e.g., UniME, mmE5, UNITE, VLM2Vec) are evaluated strictly as single-stage dual encoders. Figure 5 reveals that without reranking, FreeRet-7B achieves only ~53.7% Precision@1—well below the ~70% achieved by supervised bi-encoders. Comparing a compute-intensive two-stage system against single-stage dense retrievers without clearly separating the stages creates a misleading comparison.

Missing latency and test-time compute benchmarks: Pointwise reranking with a 7B or 32B MLLM over 50 candidate items per query entails significant computational overhead and latency compared to cosine similarity search over pre-indexed embeddings. The paper provides no concrete wall-clock time, GPU memory, or FLOPs comparisons to quantify this trade-off.

Lack of reranker baselines: To assess the true source of the gains, the paper should evaluate whether applying the proposed MLLM reranker on top of supervised embeddings (e.g., UniME or GME candidates) yields even stronger results, or compare against established multimodal rerankers rather than attributing the entire gain to the training-free paradigm.

Overstated mathematical rigor in theoretical analysis: Appendix A.2 presents Lemma 1 and Corollary A.0.1, but the argument that components orthogonal to span(W) vanish relies on heuristic assertions rather than a rigorous proof, particularly given nonlinear activation functions, intermediate layer dynamics, and regularization during pretraining.

strengths: Compelling and timely motivation: Training multimodal retrievers via contrastive fine-tuning requires massive pair curation and lacks flexibility across new backbone architectures. Demonstrating that off-the-shelf MLLMs can achieve competitive retrieval performance without any parameter updates is an important finding.

Strong empirical results: FreeRet-7B achieves 70.7% Precision@1 on the 36-dataset MMEB benchmark, matching or surpassing strong supervised models trained on millions of multimodal pairs (e.g., UniME-V2, GME, MMRet) and substantially outperforming prior training-free methods like E5-V.

Insightful probing on lexicalization pressure: The empirical investigation showing that the final MLP before the LM head sharply pulls representations toward discrete token alignment at the expense of semantic continuity is well-supported with layer-wise probing and cross-lingual synonym/antonym analysis.

Effective framing analysis for reranking: Identifying the 'LLM framing effect' (the sensitivity of pointwise reranking to logically equivalent binary label formulations such as Yes/No vs. Right/Wrong) and mitigating it using a multiple-choice question (MCQ) format provides a simple, robust practical recipe.

Extensive experimental breadth: Evaluations cover multiple model families (Qwen, InternVL, LLaVA), model sizes (2B to 32B), modality combinations (including video retrieval and LVBench long-video frame selection), cross-lingual generalization, and thorough ablation studies.
weaknesses: Reliance on task-specific prompt construction: The controlled embedding generation strategy introduces priors such as task alignment (e.g., 'You are required to assess if <placeholder> is related to <placeholder>'). It is somewhat unclear whether these prompt templates were manually tailored for each of the 36 MMEB datasets or automatically derived, which could introduce engineering overhead in open-ended settings.

Inference latency and computational cost of reranking: Even though unifying embedding and reranking into a single model saves GPU memory and reuses KV cache / vision encodings, pointwise reranking across 10 to 50 candidates using a 7B or 32B MLLM incurs substantial inference latency compared to traditional bi-encoders, limiting massive-scale candidate search without coarse pre-filtering.

Theoretical depth in Appendix C is limited: The theoretical argument presented in Lemma C.1 and Corollary C.2 is quite basic linear algebra regarding cross-entropy gradient projections onto the LM head span, offering minimal formal insight beyond what the empirical probing in Section 3.2 already illustrates.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: current multimodal retrieval systems rely heavily on expensive contrastive fine-tuning that is brittle to distribution shifts and computationally burdensome to maintain across rapidly updating MLLM backbones.

Provides insightful empirical probing into model representations: the identification of 'lexicalization pressure' at the final MLP layer (where semantic continuity drops significantly in favor of discrete token prediction) is well-supported by cosine similarity probing, cross-lingual synonym/antonym analysis, and cross-architecture validations (LLaVA, InternVL, Qwen).

Novel identification and mitigation of the 'LLM framing effect' in multimodal reranking: the paper convincingly demonstrates that semantically equivalent binary answer formats (Yes/No vs. Right/Wrong vs. MCQ) exhibit large variances due to pretraining distribution biases, and shows that MCQ framing provides substantial, stable gains.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: the framework is tested across 36 datasets in MMEB, video subsets of MMEB-V2, Flickr30K, MS-COCO, and LVBench, scaling across multiple model families (LLaVA, InternVL, Qwen) and model sizes (2B to 32B), matching or exceeding several methods trained on millions of multimodal pairs.

Careful discussion of practical trade-offs: the paper provides concrete latency and GPU memory profiling for the unified embedding and reranking pipeline (reusing vision features and KV caches), as well as a thorough qualitative error analysis.
weaknesses: Inference latency of pointwise reranking: although reusing the backbone across both stages reduces memory overhead compared to multi-model systems, evaluating the reranker on top-k candidates (e.g., $k=10$ or $k=50$) still introduces significant latency per query compared to pure dual-encoder search, which limits real-time viability in ultra-large-scale retrieval scenarios.

Heuristic nature of prompt controls: the controlled generation mechanism relies on specific prompt design templates (task alignment, semantic grounding, noise suppression). The degree to which performance depends on specific wording across unseen or highly customized retrieval domains is not fully quantified.

Simplified theoretical formulation: the theoretical justification provided in Appendix C (Lemma C.1) is fairly rudimentary and essentially re-derives the standard softmax gradient projection onto vocabulary embeddings without offering deeper technical bounds on semantic distortion.

Evaluation metric focus: the main benchmark evaluation relies primarily on Precision@1 following MMEB conventions; reporting broader ranking metrics such as NDCG@10 or MRR across all benchmark subsets would offer a more complete picture of candidate ranking quality.

strengths: Practical and well-motivated framework: The paper tackles the heavy data and compute costs of training post-hoc MLLM retrievers by proposing a fully training-free, plug-and-play two-stage retrieval pipeline.

Insightful architectural and behavioral discoveries: The identification of 'lexicalization pressure' localized in the final MLP layer and the discovery of the 'LLM framing effect' in pointwise reranking offer valuable insights into MLLM internal representations and generation biases.

Simple, effective, and parameter-free solutions: Bypassing the final MLP ($h_L^{\text{Attn}}$), controlling embedding generation via structured prompts, and framing reranking as an MCQ provide immediate and sizable empirical gains without requiring any retraining or auxiliary models.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Extensive experiments across 36 MMEB datasets, MMEB-V2 video tasks, Flickr30K, MS-COCO, and LVBench demonstrate substantial gains over prior training-free baselines (e.g., +13.9% over E5-V) and strong competitiveness against supervised models (e.g., matching or exceeding models trained on millions of multimodal pairs).

Broad generalization and thorough ablation: The authors validate the method across multiple model families (Qwen-VL, InternVL3, LLaVA-OneVision) and parameter scales (2B to 32B), as well as across languages and modalities.
weaknesses: Inference latency and candidate pool trade-off: The top performance of FreeRet relies heavily on the reranking stage ($r_{50}$ reaches 70.7% on MMEB, compared to 53.7% for embedding-only). As detailed in Appendix Table 10, reranking 50 candidates increases inference latency by more than 35x (from 0.08s to 2.97s on 7B), which may limit applicability in ultra-low-latency production retrieval systems.

Sensitivity and overhead of prompt templates: The controlled embedding generation relies on structured task priors (e.g., task alignment, semantic grounding, noise suppression). The manuscript does not systematically explore how sensitive the embeddings are to alternative phrasings or how automated prompt selection could be performed when task metadata is absent.

Overstated theoretical rigor in Appendix C: Lemma C.1 and Corollary C.2 present an elementary geometric observation regarding the gradient of the LM head projection, which overstates the formality of what is essentially an intuitive heuristic explanation of non-linear MLP behavior.

Minor typographic and formatting errors: Several typos exist in the text, such as 'reqired' and 'concent' on page 5 (Section 3.3), and in Table 8, both rows 5 and 6 are labeled as 'FreeRet_r20 Qwen2.5-VL 3B' despite having different results (row 6 appears to correspond to the 7B variant).
